title: Research questions and literature connections
purpose: A neutral, source-specific guide to the research questions addressed by the analytical note, trajectory paper and upgraded repository.
relationship_policy: Connections indicate relevant reading, not dependence, endorsement, priority, equivalence or an existing citation relationship.
source_distinction: The analytical note and the trajectory paper are distinct works. The repository is a corrected and extended companion; its later findings are not retroactively attributed to the paper.

questions.question: What does the largest eigenvalue tell us about entropy?
search_variants: entropy versus dominant eigenvalue of a density matrix
questions.answer: For a $d$-dimensional density-matrix spectrum, $p=\lambda_{\max}$ constrains entropy without determining it. The repository describes the exact finite-dimensional interval at fixed $p\in[1/d,1]$: the equal-tail spectrum maximizes Schur-concave entropies, while the spectrum packed with as many entries $p$ as possible minimizes them. This static geometry applies to spectra independently of whether a time evolution is supplied.
questions.scope: The trajectory paper supplies the original geometric viewpoint; corrected tight envelopes are documented in the repository. A random-ensemble reference curve is a different object from a feasible-region boundary. The underlying majorization tools have earlier foundations.

questions.question: How does a spectral outlier change von Neumann and Rényi entropies?
questions.answer: Write a normalized spectrum as $(p,(1-p)\mu_1,\ldots,(1-p)\mu_{d-1})$. The elementary identity $S=h_2(p)+(1-p)S(\boldsymbol\mu)$ separates the head weight from the normalized tail. The analytical note evaluates entropy relations for stated random ensembles by modeling the remaining spectral bulk. Different Rényi indices weight the outlier and the tail differently.
questions.scope: The decomposition is an elementary identity, not an originality claim. Any ensemble-specific formula still requires that ensemble’s assumptions; the dominant eigenvalue does not fix an arbitrary spectrum’s entropy.

questions.question: What happens to entanglement spectra when a random amplitude matrix has a nonzero mean?
search_variants: rank-one mean random quantum state entropy
questions.answer: A reduced state can be represented as $\rho=XX^\dagger/\operatorname{Tr}(XX^\dagger)$. For the constant-entry mean construction, the deterministic mean matrix is rank one. A nonzero mean can produce a distinguished spectral component, making outlier-and-bulk entropy analysis a useful question. The analytical note treats a non-zero-mean random-state construction; the repository separates such references from exact spectral geometry.
questions.scope: The rank-one statement concerns the specified mean construction, not all noncentral Wishart ensembles. Sampling a distribution and calculating an entropy relation are different contributions.

questions.question: How is normalized matrix-spectrum entropy connected to entanglement?
search_variants: attention matrix entropy leading singular value
questions.answer: Normalizing a matrix as $\rho=AA^\dagger/\|A\|_F^2$ turns its squared singular values into a probability spectrum. Vectorizing the same normalized matrix gives a bipartite pure state with that reduced spectrum. Consequently, a leading singular value and a diffuse tail invite the same spectral questions as a Schmidt outlier and bulk. Chen and collaborators use this connection for attention matrices.
questions.scope: This is a mathematical connection to the analytical note, not evidence that the note or repository studied language models. Results for random quantum-state ensembles do not automatically transfer to attention matrices.

questions.question: Why plot entropy against a spectral concentration instead of time?
questions.answer: The trajectory paper represents evolution through $t\mapsto(\lambda_{\max}(t),S(t))$: a joint picture of the leading weight and the rest of the spectrum. The repository compares several entropy-like projections using the same leading-weight coordinate. In Schmidt-scale transport, the maximizing-window concentration agrees with $\lambda_{\max}$ only on the branch where that window contains the leading weight alone.
questions.scope: The correspondence is branch-dependent. A time-ordered path contains chronology, whereas an unordered point cloud does not.

questions.question: Why can different entanglement measures agree globally but disagree locally?
questions.answer: At a fixed pure-state bipartition, the measures are different functions of one Schmidt spectrum. Majorization-comparable spectra are consistently ordered by Schur-concave entropies; incomparable pairs can be ordered differently by different measures. The repository tests common coarse behavior and local metric competition in its declared dataset. This distinguishes empirical agreement from mathematical equivalence.
questions.scope: Majorization is an established ordering principle. The repository’s contribution here is its use in a documented cross-metric dynamical analysis, not the introduction of majorization or a universal dynamical law.

questions.question: How can shared spectral geometry be distinguished from genuine temporal structure?
questions.answer: Jointly reordering all observables preserves their point-cloud correlations while changing temporal adjacency. The repository uses chronology controls and static matched-spectrum references to separate these questions. Its empirical common metric mode alone is not a temporal invariant. This offers a diagnostic distinction when comparing phenomenological metric agreement with a microscopic theory of common Rényi dynamics.
questions.scope: The chronology controls are follow-up repository results, not results established in the 2024 journal paper or the low-lying-modes paper.

questions.question: What can spectral trajectories show during quantum algorithms?
search_variants: Grover search entanglement evolution inside oracle
quantum Fourier transform entanglement state spectrum
questions.answer: The trajectory paper includes quantum-algorithm examples, including Grover search, and distinguishes entanglement at completed algorithmic steps from intermediate circuit structure. Joint spectral observables provide another view of how a state changes during computation. Tensor-network studies and noisy-Grover simulations provide neighboring questions about fidelity, representation and simulation cost.
questions.scope: State entanglement, operator entanglement and stochastic quantum trajectories are distinct. A global QFT need not preserve a Schmidt spectrum, and low entropy alone is not a general efficient-simulation guarantee.

neighbors.title: Artificial Entanglement in the Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models
neighbors.connection: The attention analysis uses a normalized Gram matrix with a leading spectral outlier and a diffuse bulk. Its model and application are distinct from the random ensembles in the analytical note.

neighbors.connection: Entropy–concentration paths connect to entropy–largest-eigenvalue paths when the maximizing Schmidt window contains only the leading weight. The concentration generally differs from the largest eigenvalue.

neighbors.connection: A many-body-quench setting with several information-theoretic diagnostics, including single-copy entanglement. Its physical analysis is distinct from the repository’s cross-metric comparison.

neighbors.title: Entanglement dynamics from universal low-lying modes
neighbors.connection: A replicated-dynamics explanation of common Rényi behavior, complementary to an empirical comparison of different projections of one Schmidt spectrum. The preprint is from 2024, not 2026.

neighbors.title: Efficiency of classical simulations of a noisy Grover algorithm
neighbors.connection: Algorithmic entanglement and simulation cost provide a related application. Stochastic quantum trajectories and operator entanglement are different objects from the fixed-cut pure-state spectrum path.

neighbors.title: Simulating the quantum Fourier transform, Grover's algorithm, and the quantum counting algorithm with limited entanglement using tensor-networks
